sinks.name: document.cookie
sinks.severity_note: P3 when tainted data overwrites a session/auth cookie (session fixation, token injection) or when cookie tossing on a sibling subdomain poisons the parent domain; P5 for non-security cookies (UI preferences).
sinks.explain: Assigning document.cookie = 'name=value' sets a cookie from JavaScript. When the cookie name or value comes from a tainted source (URL, postMessage, storage), an attacker controls a cookie that the browser will send with every subsequent request — enabling session fixation, CSRF-token injection, and preference-cookie attacks that flip server-side behavior.
sinks.how_it_works: Cookies set via document.cookie obey the same scoping rules as server-set ones: path and domain attributes decide where they travel. Two weapons follow. First, direct injection: tainted value lands in a cookie the server trusts (e.g. a CSRF token or session id the server does not re-validate). Second, cookie tossing: from any subdomain you can set Domain=.target.com cookies; browsers send both the attacker's cookie and the legitimate one, and many servers take the first — letting a less-trusted subdomain shadow a parent-domain cookie.
sinks.why_it_matters: Cookie writes are the quiet end of the kill chain: one document.cookie assignment can pin a victim to an attacker-known session (fixation), desync CSRF tokens, or persist tainted state that a later server-side template renders without escaping.

steps.action: Confirm a query parameter flows into a document.cookie assignment
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?theme=jlf-trace' in a browser
steps.indicator: document.cookie in the DevTools console shows a cookie containing jlf-trace

steps.action: Overwrite a security-relevant cookie with an attacker-known value
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?theme=x;sessionid=SESSION_ID' then run document.cookie in the console
steps.indicator: the sessionid cookie now holds the attacker-known SESSION_ID — if the server accepts it, the victim is fixed to the attacker's session

steps.action: Verify server-side trust in the injected cookie
steps.command: curl -s -H 'Cookie: sessionid=SESSION_ID' 'https://TARGET/account' | grep -i 'YOUR_ACCOUNT'
steps.indicator: the response renders the account tied to SESSION_ID, proving the server trusts client-writable cookie values

chains.eligibility: Session fixation via client-writable cookies is accepted when the server fails to rotate/validate the session id; injection into purely cosmetic cookies (theme, language) is informational unless chained to a stored injection.

steps.action: Demonstrate cookie tossing from a sibling subdomain
steps.command: run the payload in the console on any subdomain of TARGET, then open 'https://TARGET/' and inspect document.cookie
steps.indicator: the browser now sends two csrftoken cookies to TARGET and the shadowed value appears first in the Cookie request header

steps.action: Confirm the server accepts the tossed cookie value
steps.command: curl -s -b 'csrftoken=ATTACKER' -d 'csrfmiddlewaretoken=ATTACKER&field=1' 'https://TARGET/form'
steps.indicator: the form is accepted with the attacker-chosen token, showing the CSRF defense is defeated by the tossed cookie

chains.eligibility: Cookie tossing that defeats CSRF or session integrity is accepted on most platforms; requires control of any subdomain (takeover, XSS, or a subdomain in scope).

contexts.html-body: The cookie string itself is not rendered; impact comes from which cookie you overwrite and how the server or another page consumes it.
contexts.attr: Inject attributes into the cookie string: 'name=value; Domain=.TARGET; Path=/' widens scope; note that HttpOnly cookies cannot be read but CAN be shadowed by a same-name non-HttpOnly cookie from a subdomain.
contexts.js-string: If the value is concatenated into a string, break out of the value with ';' to append a second cookie: x;sessionid=SESSION_ID.

sinks.waf_notes: Cookie writes happen client-side; a WAF only sees the resulting Cookie header on later requests. Odd or duplicated Cookie headers in logs are the detection signal.
sinks.eligibility: Honest line: writing a cookie is only as severe as what trusts it. Session fixation, CSRF-token injection, and cross-subdomain tossing are reportable; tainted data into a preference cookie with no downstream consumer is informational.
mitigations: Never build cookie strings from untrusted input; validate names and values against an allowlist
Mark session cookies HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax/Strict, and rotate session ids at login
Use the __Host- prefix (Secure, Path=/, no Domain) so subdomains cannot shadow the cookie
Server-side: reject duplicate cookie names instead of silently taking the first

sinks.name: localStorage
sinks.severity_note: P5 for the write alone. Jumps to P2/P3 as a SECOND-ORDER chain when a stored value is later read and passed to innerHTML/eval/location.href — the read side is the real sink.
sinks.explain: localStorage.setItem(k, v) persists attacker-influenced data in the origin's long-term store (survives restarts, shared across all tabs of the origin). The write itself executes nothing — localStorage is a taint WAREHOUSE: the vulnerability detonates later, when another code path does localStorage.getItem(k) and feeds the value into a dangerous sink.
sinks.how_it_works: This is the classic source/sink pairing of second-order DOM XSS. Write side: ?name=payload -> localStorage.setItem('name', payload). Read side (different page, different session, maybe different user role): el.innerHTML = localStorage.getItem('name'). Because the store is persistent and origin-wide, the write and read can be separated by days and by pages, which is exactly why reviewers miss the chain: each half looks harmless alone.
sinks.why_it_matters: Stored DOM XSS via localStorage is self-healing against server fixes: even after the reflected parameter is patched, the poisoned value keeps detonating from the store until cleared. It is also the standard persistence mechanism for XSS worms and session-token theft.

steps.action: Confirm tainted data is written to localStorage
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?name=jlf-trace' then run localStorage in the DevTools console
steps.indicator: a localStorage entry contains jlf-trace, proving the write half of the chain

steps.action: Plant the payload and hunt the read side
steps.command: grep -n 'localStorage.getItem' app.js -A2 | grep -n 'innerHTML\|eval\|location\|write'
steps.indicator: a getItem result flows into innerHTML/eval/location.href on some page of the same origin

steps.action: Trigger the second-order detonation
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?name=' to plant it, then open the page that performs the unsafe getItem
steps.indicator: alert(document.domain) fires on the READ page with no tainted parameter in its URL — proving stored second-order XSS

chains.eligibility: Accepted as stored DOM XSS when both halves are demonstrated. A localStorage write with NO unsafe read path is informational only — always find the read-side sink before reporting.

steps.action: Identify an API response field that is cached into localStorage and later rendered
steps.command: curl -s -X PATCH -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"displayName":""}' 'https://TARGET/api/profile' --cookie 'session=SESSION_ID'
steps.indicator: a GET of https://TARGET/api/profile returns the payload unencoded in the displayName field

steps.action: Trigger the localStorage cache and the unsafe read
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/dashboard' in a browser, confirm via localStorage in the console that the payload was cached, then navigate to the page that renders it
steps.indicator: alert(document.domain) fires from the stored value with no payload in the current URL — stored second-order XSS via fetch-to-localStorage

chains.eligibility: API-to-localStorage-to-DOM is full stored XSS and accepted at XSS severity; confirm the API field lacks server-side encoding to rule out a pure server-side stored XSS duplicate.

contexts.html-body: Read side into innerHTML: stored detonates on every visit until cleared.
contexts.attr: Read side into an attribute: store a javascript: URL or an attribute-breakout string.
contexts.js-string: Read side into eval/setTimeout: store ';alert(document.domain)// style breakout content.

sinks.waf_notes: The write request may pass a WAF if the payload arrives via a parameter the WAF does not inspect (fragment, JSON body). Once stored, every detonation is client-side with zero server traffic.
sinks.eligibility: The write is never the finding — the pairing is. Storage-only findings without a demonstrated detonation path are informational on every major platform.
mitigations: Treat localStorage.getItem output as exactly as untrusted as location.search — sanitize before any DOM sink
Prefer keeping render data in memory or fetching it fresh over re-rendering from storage
Never store session tokens in localStorage (readable by any XSS on the origin); use HttpOnly cookies
references: PortSwigger: DOM-based vulnerabilities using client-side storage
OWASP WSTG: Testing for Client-side Storage

sinks.name: sessionStorage
sinks.severity_note: P5 for the write alone; P3 as a second-order chain within the same tab session. Narrower than localStorage because the store dies with the tab and is not shared across tabs.
sinks.explain: sessionStorage is the per-tab, per-session twin of localStorage: data lives only for the lifetime of the tab and is isolated between tabs. Writes are inert; the danger is the same second-order pattern — a tainted value stored now is read later in the same tab and fed into a dangerous sink.
sinks.how_it_works: Write side: a URL parameter or postMessage payload is cached via sessionStorage.setItem. Read side: a later navigation INSIDE THE SAME TAB (SPA route change, multi-step wizard, payment flow) reads the key and renders it unsafely. Because the store is tab-local, cross-tab amplification is impossible, but within a tab the stored value survives every same-tab navigation — ideal for payload delivery across wizard steps.
sinks.why_it_matters: Multi-step flows (checkout, onboarding) frequently carry state in sessionStorage between steps; one tainted write in step 1 can detonate in step 4's template, far from the injection point and invisible to server logs.

steps.action: Confirm tainted data is written to sessionStorage
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?ref=jlf-trace' then run sessionStorage in the DevTools console
steps.indicator: a sessionStorage entry contains jlf-trace, proving the write half

steps.action: Locate the same-tab read side and plant the payload
steps.command: grep -n 'sessionStorage.getItem' app.js -A2 | grep -n 'innerHTML\|eval\|location'
steps.indicator: a getItem result reaches a DOM/execution sink during a later same-tab step

steps.action: Walk the same-tab flow to the detonation point
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/page?ref=' then continue the in-tab flow (wizard steps or SPA route) to the reading page
steps.indicator: alert(document.domain) fires on the later step with no tainted parameter in its URL

chains.eligibility: Accepted as stored-in-session DOM XSS when the full same-tab chain is shown; write-only or console-only reads are informational.

steps.action: Store the payload via the router parameter
steps.command: open 'https://TARGET/app#/settings?theme=jlf-trace' and inspect sessionStorage
steps.indicator: the tainted router value lands in sessionStorage under a predictable key

steps.action: Detonate on the read side
steps.payload: payload appropriate to the read-side sink (e.g. )
steps.command: navigate to the page that reads the stored key into innerHTML (keep the same tab session)
steps.indicator: stored value renders unencoded — second-order XSS fires

chains.eligibility: Second-order storage XSS is accepted on major platforms when you show the full write->read->detonate path in one session. Storage write alone without a sink is Informational.

contexts.html-body: Read side into innerHTML: stored .
contexts.attr: Read side into an attribute: javascript: URL or breakout string.

sinks.waf_notes: Same blindness as localStorage, plus the store never crosses the network at all — there is no server artifact of the stored payload.
sinks.eligibility: Same rule as localStorage: the pairing is the finding. Tab isolation makes cross-victim impact harder to demonstrate, so document the exact same-tab navigation path in the report.
mitigations: Sanitize sessionStorage reads before any DOM sink — same-tab storage is not a trust boundary
Pass wizard state server-side or via signed tokens instead of client storage
Clear sensitive sessionStorage keys on logout/route exit
references: PortSwigger: DOM-based vulnerabilities using client-side storage
OWASP WSTG: Testing for Client-side Storage

sinks.name: window.name
sinks.severity_note: P3 when window.name is read into a DOM/execution sink — it is the one client-side store that survives CROSS-ORIGIN navigation, so any attacker page can plant it.
sinks.explain: window.name is a string property of the browsing context that — uniquely among client-side stores — persists across navigations INCLUDING cross-origin ones. A page that writes window.name = tainted data, or one that reads window.name into a sink, is dealing with a value any previously-visited website could have planted.
sinks.how_it_works: The name belongs to the tab, not the origin. Attack: attacker.com sets window.name = payload then does location = 'https://TARGET/page'. The navigation crosses origins but the tab keeps its name; TARGET's code reads window.name and writes it to innerHTML — the payload detonates in TARGET's origin. No parameter, no storage permission, no server log. Historically window.name was also abused as a cross-domain transport, so legacy code often treats it as trusted.
sinks.why_it_matters: It is the stealthiest DOM XSS source: the payload arrives via a navigation that looks completely clean in TARGET's access logs (no query string, no fragment, a same-site referrer or none), which defeats both WAFs and incident response.

steps.action: Confirm the target reads window.name into a sink
steps.command: grep -n 'window.name' app.js -A2 | grep -n 'innerHTML\|eval\|write\|location'
steps.indicator: window.name flows into innerHTML/eval/document.write/location.href without sanitization

steps.action: Build a planter page that sets window.name and navigates to the target
steps.command: host at https://ATTACKER/plant.html and open it in a browser
steps.indicator: the browser lands on https://TARGET/page and alert(document.domain) fires — the payload crossed origins inside window.name

steps.action: Prove no server-side trace exists
steps.command: curl -s 'https://TARGET/page' -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' and compare with the access log for the victim request
steps.indicator: the victim's request to TARGET contained no payload in path or query — confirming server-side controls cannot see this vector

chains.eligibility: window.name DOM XSS is accepted on major platforms because the cross-origin planting is fully attacker-controlled; note in the report that the attack requires the victim to visit the planter page first (one-click or drive-by).

steps.action: Plant the payload in window.name from an attacker page
steps.command: host poc.html on https://ATTACKER that sets window.name then navigates to the target
steps.indicator: after cross-origin navigation, the target reads window.name — your payload survived

steps.action: Confirm detonation in the target's sink
steps.command: watch the target page render
steps.indicator: payload executes in the TARGET origin — full cross-origin DOM XSS

chains.eligibility: window.name XSS is a well-accepted vector (survives cross-origin navigation). Rate it like any DOM XSS (P2-P3) when the sink read is shown.

contexts.attr: window.name into an attribute: javascript: URL or breakout.

sinks.waf_notes: The definitive WAF-blind vector: the payload never appears in any HTTP request to the target. Only client-side defenses (CSP on the final sink, sanitization) can stop it.
sinks.eligibility: Reportable DOM XSS when a sink pairing exists. A page that only WRITES window.name from tainted data is a taint carrier, not a finding, until you find a page that reads it unsafely (often a different page of the same app).
mitigations: Never read window.name into a DOM or execution sink; treat it as attacker-controlled on every page load
If window.name must be used (legacy transport), validate its exact expected format before use and clear it afterwards
Modern replacement: use sessionStorage or postMessage with origin checks instead of window.name transport
